definitions.definition: Something that exists first and is the foundation for everything else.
definitions.example: If math is ontologically prior to matter, then math existed before the universe and the universe is built from math.

definitions.definition: Two different ways of looking at the same underlying thing.
definitions.example: A 3D object can be projected as a shadow on a wall or as a drawing on paper; both are different views of the same object.

definitions.definition: A pattern or set of rules that stays the same even when everything around it changes.
definitions.example: The number of sides on a square is invariant no matter how big or small the square is.

definitions.definition: The belief that abstract ideas like numbers and sets are just names humans made up, not real things that exist on their own.
definitions.example: A nominalist says the number 2 is just a label we use, not a real object floating in space.

definitions.definition: The belief that abstract ideas like numbers and shapes are real things that exist in a non-physical world outside space and time.
definitions.example: A Platonist says the perfect circle exists in an ideal realm, even though no perfect circle exists in the physical world.

definitions.definition: Unable to cause any physical effect or change.
definitions.example: A thought in your head is causally inert because it cannot push a rock by itself.

definitions.definition: The belief that mathematical statements are not really true, but we pretend they are because they are useful.
definitions.example: A fictionalist says '2+2=4' is a useful fiction, like saying 'the sun rises' even though the sun doesn't actually rise.

definitions.definition: Something that could be different or might not exist at all; dependent on something else.
definitions.example: The fact that you are reading this is contingent — you could have chosen to do something else.

definitions.definition: Something that must be true and cannot be false in any possible situation.
definitions.example: That a triangle has three sides is necessary — it cannot be otherwise.

definitions.definition: Never changing; always the same.
definitions.example: The fact that 2+2=4 is immutable — it was true a billion years ago and will be true a billion years from now.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or substance that something is made of or depends on.
definitions.example: Paper is the substrate for a printed book; a brain is the substrate for a thought.

definitions.definition: Incapable of being wrong; always correct.
definitions.example: A simple calculator is infallible for basic arithmetic if used correctly.

definitions.definition: When two things belong to completely different types or categories, so they cannot be the same kind of thing.
definitions.example: Saying an apple and a dream are the same is a categorical mismatch because one is physical and the other is mental.

definitions.definition: The principle that the simplest explanation with the fewest assumptions is usually the best.
definitions.example: If you hear hoofbeats, parsimony says think horses, not zebras.

definitions.definition: The process of stating the basic rules (axioms) from which all other truths in a system can be derived.
definitions.example: Euclid's geometry was axiomatized by starting with a few simple rules like 'a straight line can be drawn between any two points.'

definitions.definition: A rule that says the strength of a force (like gravity) gets weaker by the square of the distance from its source.
definitions.example: If you are twice as far from a light bulb, the light is only one-fourth as bright.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the second law of thermodynamics says entropy always increases over time.
definitions.example: A messy room has higher entropy than a tidy one, and it naturally gets messier without effort.

definitions.definition: An argument that avoids the real issue by playing with the meaning of words instead of addressing the facts.
definitions.example: Saying 'water isn't wet because wet means something that makes other things wet' is a semantic dodge.

definitions.definition: A type of geometry where the rules are different from the usual ones taught in school, like on a curved surface instead of a flat one.
definitions.example: On a globe, the shortest path between two points is a curve, not a straight line — that's non-Euclidean geometry.

definitions.definition: Numbers that include the square root of negative one (i), allowing solutions to equations that have no real number solutions.
definitions.example: The number 3 + 2i is a complex number; it is used in electronics and quantum physics.

definitions.definition: A branch of mathematics that studies symmetry and the ways objects can be transformed while keeping their structure.
definitions.example: Group theory explains why a snowflake has six-fold symmetry.

definitions.definition: A specific example or physical version of an abstract idea or pattern.
definitions.example: A particular red apple is an instantiation of the abstract concept 'redness.'

definitions.definition: Kurt Gödel, a mathematician who proved that in any consistent mathematical system, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.example: Gödel showed that math can never fully prove itself, like a camera that cannot take a picture of itself.

definitions.definition: Alfred Tarski, a logician who proved that no language can define what 'truth' means within that same language.
definitions.example: Tarski showed that English cannot fully define 'truth' using only English words.

definitions.definition: Alan Turing, a mathematician who proved that there is no general method to determine whether a computer program will ever finish running or run forever.
definitions.example: Turing showed you cannot write a program that checks if any other program will get stuck in an infinite loop.

definitions.definition: Rolf Landauer, a physicist who proved that erasing information always produces a tiny amount of heat, setting a minimum energy cost for computing.
definitions.example: Every time you delete a file on a computer, a tiny bit of heat is released because of Landauer's principle.

definitions.definition: When multiple independent lines of evidence or arguments all point to the same conclusion without being designed to do so.
definitions.example: If a detective, a reporter, and a witness all independently describe the same suspect, that is unforced convergence.

definitions.definition: Specific conditions that, if met, would prove a theory or claim is wrong.
definitions.example: A claim that 'all swans are white' has a falsification criterion: find one black swan.

definitions.definition: The ability to cause physical effects or changes in the world.
definitions.example: A rock has causal efficacy because it can break a window; a thought does not.

definitions.definition: The ability to make choices and act intentionally.
definitions.example: A human has agency; a rock does not.
